prize_parts.citation: for establishing, through kinetic measurements on modified proteins, the physical principles of long-range electron transfer in biological molecules
for the chemical strategy of covalently targeting the KRAS G12C switch-II pocket, making a long-intractable oncogene druggable

statement.case_for: B067 states a biological question in physical terms: Gray and Winkler measured electron-transfer rates in ruthenium-modified proteins with time-resolved kinetics, showed how rate depends on distance and on the intervening medium, and later developed the hopping picture. That framework underlies how respiratory and photosynthetic enzymes move charge. The experimental attribution is clean, the results have been confirmed across many proteins and independent groups for decades, and recognition would not be premature. B066 is the other part because it has the cleanest attribution on the list: one laboratory found the cryptic switch-II pocket and the tethering-based covalent chemistry, and approved KRAS G12C drugs followed. Together the two parts keep the union at three people and reward mechanism-level chemistry with a sharply attributable discovery.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation about B067 is that the foundations of electron-transfer theory (Marcus, and the Hopfield and Beratan-Onuchic tunneling-pathway work) were recognized earlier or sit outside the credited pair, so the committee must show that the protein-kinetics program is a distinct achievement and not a late extension of earlier prizes. Opening support was thin: only I ranked it first. B066 may be viewed as a single drug-discovery success on one target, and its clinical durability is still being studied. A two-part prize of this kind combines two fairly unrelated topics and does not match the broad momentum behind B036.

responses.point: Aili ranks B036 first because hijacking the ubiquitin-proteasome system with PROTACs and molecular glues created a designable chemical modality, with Crews, Deshaies and Handa as the trio.
responses.response: I agree the principle is real and the impact is large, and B036 is on my list. My reservation is attribution and maturity. PROTACs and molecular glues are two threads with different discoverers, and the trio leaves out Ciulli, Gray and Sakamoto. No degrader has yet been approved, so the clinical argument rests on trials. The expert reports should settle whether the field is one discovery or two before we commit three names. I would not set it aside, which is why I list it as an alternative, but I do not think the case is as clean as the opening support suggests.

responses.point: Aqvist ranks B023 first: energy-landscape and funnel theory, with Fersht's phi-value experiments, turned protein folding into a quantitative physical-chemical framework.
responses.response: I share the wish for physical principles that connect quantitatively to experiment, and that is why I weigh B067 so heavily. But B023 has the attribution problem Johan himself notes: Dill and Bryngelson fall outside a trio, and I cannot tell which share belongs to theory and which to experiment. The 2024 prize also overlaps in protein structure. I would put B023 behind B067, where the experimental core is two named people and the measurements are decisive.

responses.point: Linke, the chair, ranks B014 first: liquid-liquid phase separation as an organizing principle of cells, with Hyman, Brangwynne and Rosen as founders.
responses.response: It is an appealing physical idea, and I accept the founding observation. My concern is the one Heiner raises himself: whether many reported condensates are equilibrium phase separation or other assemblies is still disputed, so the mechanism is less settled than for protein electron transfer or covalent KRAS targeting. I would want the expert report to show which in vivo claims have been tested quantitatively before we give it first place.

responses.point: Zou ranks B017 first: surfactant-templated ordered mesoporous silica, credited to Kresge and Beck with Ryoo, as a new class of porous solids.
responses.response: The originality and maturity are not in doubt, and thirty years of replication is a strong argument. The priority question with Inagaki's FSM-16 is the weak point, and the committee cannot ignore it when a three-person limit already excludes Stucky and Zhao. I would also consider how soon after the MOF and COF prize it would come. I do not rank it among my top choices, but I would like to hear how Xiaodong weighs the FSM-16 priority.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat protein electron transfer (B067) as a distinct discovery after earlier electron-transfer recognition.
Whether the expert reports treat PROTACs and molecular glues as one achievement or two, and whether clinical approval is needed first.
Whether Shokat's single-laureate part is enough, or whether the KRAS work should be combined with other covalent-drug contributors.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for the shortlisted candidates. As Secretary I note that I work in the same field as B067 (biological electron and proton transfer) and have a Stockholm University colleague on the committee (Zou), but neither is a personal or institutional connection to any credited name.
